content.text: How to use this chapter

content.body:
Most shoulder teaching is a list of tests and a list of treatments. That produces a resident who can recite Hawkins-Kennedy and cannot write a rehabilitation programme.

This chapter is built the other way round. Every section answers the same underlying question — what is this tendon's capacity, what load is it being asked to carry, and which of the two am I going to change? The anatomy is here because it tells you what to train. The pathophysiology is here because it tells you how fast you can progress. The examination is here because each finding changes a line in the prescription.

Sections 3 and 4 (anatomy and biomechanics; pathophysiology) and section 11 (the loading programme) are the same idea told twice — once as biology, once as a prescription pad. Read them together.

content.text: 1. Introduction, definition and the reasoning model
1.1 The condition in one paragraph

content.body: Rotator cuff tendinopathy is a painful, load-related disorder of the rotator cuff tendons and the tissues immediately around them, in which the demand placed on the tendon has exceeded its capacity to tolerate that demand. It is the commonest cause of shoulder pain across the lifespan, it is overwhelmingly a problem of tendon capacity rather than of bony geometry, its structural findings on imaging correlate only loosely with symptoms, and its primary treatment is progressive mechanical loading delivered over months. Everything else in this chapter elaborates that sentence.

content.text: 1.2 A working definition

content.body: A definition is only useful if it tells you what is in and what is out. The one below is the one to carry into clinic.

content.label: Definition
content.text: Rotator cuff tendinopathy — a clinical syndrome of shoulder pain and loss of function, characteristically provoked by load and by elevation, arising from the rotator cuff tendons, their enthesis and the adjacent subacromial–subdeltoid bursa, in which the underlying tissue change is degenerative and failed-adaptive rather than primarily inflammatory, and in which symptoms are only loosely coupled to structural findings.

content.body: What that definition deliberately contains:

rows: Calcific disease is a distinct subtype with a different procedural pathway, but it sits inside the same umbrella
Mechanically and clinically continuous with tendinopathy; managed the same way
The bursa is a major pain source and is rarely diseased in isolation
Anatomically and clinically inseparable in most patients

content.body: What sits outside it:

rows: A different pathway with a time-critical surgical decision (4.14, 13.2)
A mechanical problem of lost fulcrum, needing a specific programme (13.5)
Capsular, not tendinous; globally restricted passive range

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Tendinopathy is a diagnosis of pattern, not of imaging.
The three features that define it clinically are load-related pain, elevation-related pain, and pain that is reasonably reproducible for a given load. If all three are absent, no scan report should persuade you that the cuff is the problem — and if all three are present, no normal scan should persuade you that it is not.
1.3 Why the name keeps changing

content.body: This matters because the terminology tells you which model of the disease the speaker is using — and most residents learn the old one first.

rows: Neer (1972): the acromion mechanically abrades the cuff from outside
The tendon itself is the problem — degenerative, load-related
Accurate but narrow; ignores bursa, capsule, kinematics
Umbrella term: a presentation, not a single structural lesion
The current preferred term in much of the literature

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The shift from "impingement" to "rotator cuff related shoulder pain" is not pedantry — it changes what you do.
"Impingement" implies something is being pinched, which implies something should be unpinched. That logic drove decades of subacromial decompression surgery. When that surgery was finally tested against placebo surgery, it did not outperform it.
"Rotator cuff related shoulder pain" implies a tissue whose capacity has fallen below the load being asked of it — which implies you either reduce the load, build the capacity, or both. That is a rehabilitation problem, and it is why this condition belongs to PM&R.
Use whichever term your department uses, but know which model you are reasoning from. The model determines your first sentence to the patient, and the first sentence determines a surprising amount of the outcome.
1.4 Where it sits among shoulder disorders

rows: Tendinopathy (± calcific) · partial-thickness tear · bursopathy · long head of biceps tendinopathy · degenerative full-thickness tear · traumatic full-thickness tear → surgical pathway · massive / irreparable tear → specific programme

content.body: Roughly two-thirds to 70% of shoulder presentations fall in the left-hand branch. The clinical skill is not in recognising that branch — it is in placing the patient correctly within it, because the sub-branches have genuinely different management.

content.text: 1.5 Why this condition belongs to PM&R

content.body: Four reasons, worth being able to state:

rows: The definitive treatment is a graded exercise programme
It needs someone who can prescribe, dose and progress load — not just recommend "physio"
The decisive assessment is functional, not structural
Capacity, irritability, movement quality and target load are physiatric assessments
The dominant surgical procedure failed placebo testing
Outcome depends heavily on beliefs, work and comorbidity
It needs a whole-person, function-oriented approach

content.text: 1.6 The capacity–load model, stated properly

content.body: Every tendinopathy — cuff, Achilles, patellar, gluteal — can be written as a single inequality:
Symptoms arise when demand placed on the tendon ÷ capacity of the tendon > 1

This looks trivial. It is not, because it generates the entire management plan and it forces you to be specific about both halves.

The numerator — demand — has four components, and they are independently modifiable:

columns: How a patient changes it without noticing
rows: A new heavier toolbag; a 4 kg instead of 2 kg dumbbell
Decorating a house over a weekend
How often, and how much recovery between
Six overhead shifts in a row instead of three
Where in range, and how fast the load is applied
Working above shoulder height; starting throwing again

content.body: The denominator — capacity — also has four components:

rows: Collagen quantity, organisation, cross-linking, cross-sectional area
Cuff, deltoid, scapular and trunk musculature
Age, glycaemic control, smoking, sleep, oestrogen status, medication

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Two questions for every patient, every time:
  1. What changed about the load? (new job, new training block, a weekend of painting, a child who now needs lifting, a shoulder being used to compensate for the other one)
  2. What changed about the tissue? (a birthday, a diagnosis of diabetes, a year of deconditioning, a period of illness, the menopause, a course of fluoroquinolones)
One of them nearly always has. If you cannot answer either, you either have not asked properly or you have the wrong diagnosis.
1.7 The spectrum of structural change

content.body:
1. Normal tendon
  2. Reactive tendinopathy — load exceeds capacity, tendon responds
  3. Tendon dysrepair — failed healing, matrix disorganisation begins
  4. Degenerative tendinopathy — established matrix breakdown, cell death, neovessels
  5. Partial-thickness tear (articular-side, bursal-side or intrasubstance)
  6. Full-thickness tear
  7. Massive / irreparable tear ± cuff tear arthropathy

Three caveats about that sequence, and residents should be able to state all three.

It is not an inevitable progression. Most tendinopathy never becomes a tear. The arrows are possibilities, not a conveyor belt, and saying otherwise to a patient installs a fear that will shape their behaviour for years.

Pain does not track the structural stage. Patients with full-thickness tears can be pain-free and functional; patients with structurally normal imaging can be severely disabled. Structure and symptoms are loosely coupled, which is the single most useful fact in the whole chapter.

The stages are not uniform within one tendon. A degenerative tendon usually has normal tissue around the abnormal area. This matters enormously for treatment and is explained in 4.10.

content.text: 1.8 The four questions that structure every consultation

content.body: By the end of the first appointment you should be able to answer these. If you cannot, your plan will be generic.

rows: 1. Is this the cuff at all?
History pattern, passive range, cervical screen, neurological pattern
2. Is there structural failure that changes the pathway?
Lag signs, trauma history, weakness disproportionate to pain, age
Whether this is a surgical conversation
3. How irritable is it right now?
Pain at rest, night pain, how little it takes to provoke, how long it takes to settle
4. What is the target load they need to get back to?

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Questions 3 and 4 are the ones that distinguish a physiatrist from a diagnostician.
Anyone can label the tendon. The clinically useful work is deciding the starting dose from irritability and defining the finishing load from the patient's life. The programme is simply the bridge between those two numbers.
A 68-year-old who needs to reach a high kitchen shelf and a 24-year-old volleyball spiker have the same diagnosis and completely different endpoints. Section 11 is about building that bridge.
2. Epidemiology and risk — reading a risk-factor list as a treatment list
2.1 The burden

content.body:
• Shoulder pain is the third commonest musculoskeletal presentation in primary care, after low back and neck pain.
  • Rotator cuff disorders account for roughly two-thirds to 70% of shoulder pain presentations.
  • Prevalence rises steeply with age, and supraspinatus is involved most often.
  • A substantial proportion of patients still have symptoms at 12 months, which is why early, correct framing matters more than early intervention.

content.text: 2.2 Risk factors

rows: Age (the strongest single factor) · genetic predisposition (familial clustering is well described) · dominant arm
Overhead work · repetitive loading · vibration · sustained static postures · sudden increases in training or work volume
Prior shoulder trauma · glenohumeral or AC joint pathology · critical shoulder angle >35°
Low recovery expectation · fear-avoidance · distress · job dissatisfaction · compensation context

content.text: 2.3 How to actually use that table

content.body: A risk-factor list is only useful if you convert it into clinical actions. Residents tend to recite it and then ignore it. Read it in three columns instead:

rows: Adjust the predicted recovery duration; do not promise a 20-year-old's timeline to a 65-year-old
This is what you modify in week one, and what you rebuild capacity for by week twelve
Determines the rate of adaptation and the likelihood of a good outcome
These are active treatment targets, not background

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Treat the metabolic risk factors as part of the treatment, not as background history.
Diabetes roughly doubles the risk of rotator cuff disease and is associated with poorer outcomes after both conservative and surgical treatment. Hyperglycaemia drives advanced glycation end-product cross-linking of collagen, which makes tendon stiffer, more brittle and less able to remodel. Smoking impairs tendon perfusion and healing and is associated with larger tears and worse repair outcomes.
A patient with recalcitrant cuff pain, an HbA1c of 78 mmol/mol and a 20-pack-year history is not a rehabilitation failure — they are being asked to heal tendon in a hostile metabolic environment. Say so, write it in the letter, and treat it as part of the plan.

content.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content.text:
Do not reflexively attribute tendinopathy in a patient on a fluoroquinolone or a statin to the drug.
Fluoroquinolone tendinopathy is real but predominantly affects the Achilles, is more common in older patients, in renal impairment and with concurrent corticosteroid, and typically appears within weeks of exposure. Statin association is weak and inconsistent.
Note the drug, consider stopping a fluoroquinolone if the temporal relationship is convincing, and then still do the load assessment. Attributing everything to a tablet is how a load problem goes unmanaged for six months.
3. Anatomy and biomechanics

content.body: The shoulder anatomy chapter covers this ground in full. What follows is a working review, written so that every structure is followed by the reason it matters clinically. If you can explain 3.9 to 3.13 to a colleague, you can design a rehabilitation programme from first principles.

content.text: 3.1 The shoulder complex in overview

content.body: The shoulder is not a joint. It is four joints working as a linked system, and the cuff operates at the point where the system is least constrained.

rows: Ball and socket, minimal bony constraint
The main contributor to elevation (~120° of 180°)
Not a true joint — a muscular articulation
~60° of elevation via upward rotation; positions the glenoid
Transmits load from scapula to clavicle; permits scapular rotation
Saddle, the only bony link to the axial skeleton
Elevation, retraction and rotation of the clavicle

content.body: The trade-off that defines shoulder pathology: the glenoid holds roughly a third of the humeral head surface, with a capsule that is lax in mid-range. The shoulder buys the largest range of motion in the body at the cost of bony stability — and the bill is paid by dynamic stabilisers. The rotator cuff is the principal payer.

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
The shoulder is a golf ball on a tee. The cuff is the hand holding it there.
Every consequence in this chapter follows from that: why the cuff is load-bearing rather than merely motor, why fatigue and weakness produce mechanical failure rather than just slowness, and why the treatment is strengthening.
3.2 The four muscles — a structured review

rows: Compression of the head into the glenoid; abduction throughout the arc, with deltoid
Middle facet, extending onto the superior facet
External rotation (the main contributor); posterior compression; depression
External rotation, especially in abduction; inferior stabilisation
Internal rotation; the only anterior restraint; head depression via lower fibres

content.body:
Points worth knowing beyond the table:

  • Subscapularis is the largest and strongest cuff muscle — roughly as large as the other three combined by cross-sectional area. It is also the most frequently under-tested and under-loaded in rehabilitation.
  • Supraspinatus and infraspinatus share one nerve. Isolated infraspinatus wasting therefore suggests a lesion distal to the spinoglenoid notch — classically a spinoglenoid cyst — rather than generalised cuff disease.
  • Teres minor is axillary-innervated, which is why it is often preserved in suprascapular neuropathy and why Hornblower's sign has localising value.
  • The cuff muscles are densely spindled and highly proprioceptive, consistent with a stabilising rather than a purely motor role.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Innervation patterns are your fastest route to a neurological diagnosis.

rows: Suprascapular nerve at the spinoglenoid notch — image for a cyst
Deltoid + teres minor, sensory loss over the lateral shoulder
Cuff weakness with biceps and brachioradialis involvement

content.body: Each of these is mistaken for cuff tendinopathy routinely. The discriminator is that these produce weakness disproportionate to pain, while tendinopathy produces pain disproportionate to weakness.

content.text: 3.3 The tendons, the footprint and the enthesis

content.body:
The four tendons do not insert as four separate straps. They blend into a continuous sheet over the humeral head, interdigitating with the joint capsule beneath and the bursa above — which is why isolated "pure" single-tendon pathology is uncommon and why tear patterns cross classical boundaries.

The footprint:

rows: Footprint smaller than classically taught — roughly 1–1.5 cm in anteroposterior width at the tuberosity
Part of what is reported as "supraspinatus" is infraspinatus
Broad, with the superior third most frequently torn

content.body: The enthesis — the tendon-to-bone transition — has four zones:

This graded transition exists to spread stress across a junction between two materials of vastly different stiffness. Two clinical consequences follow:

  1. The enthesis is a stress concentrator — and therefore a common site of degenerative change and of tear initiation.
  2. Surgical repair does not recreate it. It heals with fibrovascular scar, which is weaker. This is the biological reason behind re-tear rates and the three-month delay before strengthening after repair (13.3).

content.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content.text:
Anterosuperior tears are commonly under-called. Because infraspinatus extends onto the superior facet, and because subscapularis tears are frequently partial and involve only the upper third, a tear described as "supraspinatus" may involve more than the report implies.
A medially dislocated long head of biceps is a subscapularis tear until proven otherwise — the subscapularis tendon forms the medial wall of the bicipital pulley.
Clinical consequence: test subscapularis properly (belly press, bear hug, lift-off) in every patient with anterior shoulder pain, and do not accept "supraspinatus tendinopathy" as a complete account of an anterosuperior presentation.
3.4 The rotator interval, the biceps pulley and the long head of biceps

content.body:
The rotator interval is the triangular gap between the anterior border of supraspinatus and the superior border of subscapularis. It is not empty — it contains the coracohumeral ligament, the superior glenohumeral ligament, and the long head of biceps tendon passing through on its way to the supraglenoid tubercle.

Those structures form the biceps pulley, a sling that holds the long head in its groove.

rows: Restrains inferior translation and external rotation in adduction
Thickens and contracts in adhesive capsulitis — the reason ER is lost first
Contested; probably a head depressor and pain generator more than a prime mover
Anterior pain; may hypertrophy in cuff deficiency

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The long head of biceps is a reliable pain generator and an unreliable anatomical innocent.
It is richly innervated, frequently inflamed alongside cuff disease, and a common reason anterior shoulder pain persists after the cuff settles. Treat it as a companion diagnosis rather than a competing one: test it (Speed's, palpation in the groove with the arm in 10° internal rotation), and remember that a medially subluxed biceps on ultrasound points to a subscapularis lesion, not an isolated biceps problem.
3.5 The rotator cable and crescent

content.body:
The rotator cable is a thickened band of fibres running perpendicular to the supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons, spanning from the biceps anchor anteriorly to the inferior infraspinatus posteriorly. The thinner tissue it spans is the crescent.

Burkhart's suspension bridge model: the cable transmits load around the crescent, so a tear within the crescent may be mechanically compensated while the cable is intact.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
This explains an otherwise puzzling observation: some patients with substantial tears function remarkably well. If the cable is intact, load is transmitted around the defect, the fulcrum is preserved, and the shoulder continues to work.
It is the anatomical argument for treating the patient's function, not the size of the hole on the report — and the anatomical reason you should never write a patient off on the basis of tear dimensions alone.
3.6 How a tendon is built — microstructure and matrix

content.body:
You cannot understand what degenerates unless you know what is there. This subsection feeds directly into section 4.

The hierarchy, smallest to largest:

1. Collagen molecule (tropocollagen, triple helix)
  2. Microfibril → fibril (the load-bearing unit)
  3. Fibre (tenocytes lie in rows between fibres)
  4. Fascicle (bounded by endotenon, carrying vessels and nerves)
  5. Tendon (bounded by epitenon, then paratenon)
The composition:

rows: Tensile strength. Highly cross-linked, aligned along the line of pull
Thinner, weaker, less cross-linked. Rises in tendinopathy and healing
Bind water, control fibril spacing and sliding. Aggrecan rises where tendon is compressed
Sense load and maintain the matrix

content.body: The crimp. At rest, collagen fibrils lie in a regular wave pattern. Taking up that crimp is what produces the compliant "toe region" of the stress–strain curve (4.6). Crimp is lost with age and with degeneration, which shifts the tendon's behaviour and reduces its ability to absorb low loads without strain.

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Collagen carries the load; proteoglycans manage water and sliding; tenocytes run the factory.
Tendinopathy is best understood as the factory responding badly: tenocytes over-produce proteoglycan and type III collagen, water is drawn in, the tendon swells, fibril organisation is lost, and the structure gets worse at carrying tension — which is exactly the picture in 4.8.
3.7 Blood supply and innervation

content.body:
Blood supply comes from the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries, the suprascapular artery and the thoracoacromial branches, entering through the musculotendinous junction, the bone at the insertion, and the surrounding paratenon.

Codman described a hypovascular "critical zone" approximately 1 cm proximal to the supraspinatus insertion.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
The critical zone is less settled than textbooks suggest. Some later studies have found normal or even increased vascularity in that region, and tendinopathic tendons frequently show neovascularisation rather than ischaemia.
Teach it as a historical concept with plausible relevance to a watershed region, not as established pathophysiology. The better-supported vascular statement is that tendon blood supply declines with age and with metabolic disease — which is one of the mechanisms behind the risk factors in 2.2, and a reason adaptation is slower in the patients you see most.
Innervation. Healthy tendon mid-substance is sparsely innervated, with most nerve supply in the paratenon, the bursa and the enthesis. The bursa in particular is densely innervated and is a major nociceptive source. In tendinopathy, new vessels growing into the tendon are accompanied by new nerve fibres, which is one explanation for pain arising from tissue that should barely feel anything (4.12).
3.8 The subacromial space and the bursa

content.body:
The coracoacromial arch is formed by the acromion, the coracoacromial ligament and the coracoid process. Beneath it pass the supraspinatus tendon, the long head of biceps and the bursa.

  • Acromiohumeral interval: normally 7–14 mm. Below 7 mm indicates superior migration of the humeral head — a marker of a large or massive tear, not simple tendinopathy.
  • The subacromial–subdeltoid bursa is the largest in the body. It does not normally communicate with the joint, so fluid in both the joint and the bursa suggests a full-thickness tear.
  • Critical shoulder angle >35° is associated with cuff tears; <30° with glenohumeral osteoarthritis.

The bursa's real job is to allow the cuff to glide under the arch with minimal friction. It is a synovial structure, capable of thickening, producing effusion and becoming a significant pain source — and it is the target of a subacromial injection, which is why the needle goes into the bursa and never into the tendon.

The space narrows physiologically during elevation. That is normal, happens in asymptomatic shoulders, and is not in itself pathology. Proximity is not pathology.

content.text: 3.9 Biomechanics I — concavity compression and the fulcrum

content.body:
This is the central mechanical concept of the chapter.

The glenoid is shallow, so stability cannot come from bony capture. It comes from concavity compression: the cuff pulls the humeral head into the concavity of the glenoid (deepened by the labrum), and the resulting compressive force resists translation in every direction. The deeper the concavity and the greater the compression, the greater the shear force the joint can resist before the head slides.

The cuff is therefore a compressor before it is a mover.

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text: Abandon the teaching that "supraspinatus initiates the first 15° of abduction." It is active across the whole arc, its dominant function is compression, and many patients with isolated supraspinatus tears abduct fully.

content.body:
Why this matters clinically. Deltoid's line of pull in the early arc is largely vertical. Without cuff compression to hold the head centred, deltoid translates the head superiorly instead of rotating it about a fixed centre. Cuff dysfunction therefore produces a loss of the fulcrum — painful, inefficient, substituted movement with a shrugging pattern — rather than frank paralysis.

Why this matters for the programme. If the deficit is a failure of compression, exercise selection should produce compression under control, not only isolated rotational strength. This is the rationale for including closed-chain and axially loaded work — wall press, quadruped weight shift, loaded carries — alongside classic open-chain band work.

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Deltoid is the engine. The cuff is the wheel bearing.
A powerful engine with a failed bearing does not produce speed; it produces noise, heat and wear. That is exactly what a cuff-deficient shoulder looks like on examination.
3.10 Biomechanics II — the force couples

content.body: A force couple is two forces acting in different directions to produce rotation without translation. The shoulder has three that matter.

rows: Deltoid (superior pull) balanced by the inferior cuff — subscapularis (lower fibres), infraspinatus, teres minor
Unopposed deltoid → superior migration, loss of fulcrum, pseudoparalysis in the extreme
Subscapularis anteriorly balanced by infraspinatus + teres minor posteriorly
Imbalance → anteroposterior instability of the head during rotation; this is the couple that must stay balanced for a tear to remain functional
Upper trapezius + serratus anterior + lower trapezius producing upward rotation; rhomboids and levator opposing
Loss of upward rotation → the scapula fails to position the glenoid for elevation

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Burkhart's insight: a cuff tear is functionally tolerable if the force couples remain balanced.
This is why tear size predicts function poorly. A tear that spares the transverse couple — leaving subscapularis anteriorly and infraspinatus posteriorly intact and opposed — allows the head to stay centred, and the patient often elevates well. A tear that unbalances it, typically by extending into infraspinatus, produces the clinically unstable, poorly functioning shoulder.
When you prescribe external rotation work, you are not training "the external rotators" — you are restoring the balancing arm of a couple. That is why a programme of nothing but band external rotation is incomplete, and why a programme with no external rotation at all is wrong.
3.11 Biomechanics III — the scapula and scapulohumeral rhythm

content.body:
Elevation of the arm to 180° is produced by roughly 120° at the glenohumeral joint and 60° of scapular upward rotation, conventionally described as a 2:1 ratio. The ratio is not constant — the first 30° is predominantly glenohumeral, and the scapular contribution increases through the arc — so treat 2:1 as a teaching average, not a measurement.

What the scapula contributes, and why each matters:

rows: Keeps the glenoid under the humeral head as the arm elevates
Loss of the stable base; the humeral head loses its socket at the top of range
Elevates the acromion away from the cuff during elevation
The cuff originates on the scapula — if the scapula moves, the cuff's origin is unstable
The cuff works from a moving platform and cannot generate stable compression

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The cuff originates on the scapula. That single fact justifies scapular training.
A muscle cannot produce stable compression if its origin is unstable. This is the mechanical argument for serratus anterior and lower trapezius work in a cuff programme — not a general enthusiasm for "posture".
It also sets the limit on that argument: scapular dyskinesis is common in asymptomatic people, and its association with pain is weaker than commonly taught (6.6). Train the scapula because the symptom-modification test was positive, not because it looked unusual.
3.12 Biomechanics IV — moment arms, position and the loads the cuff carries

content.body: Moment arms change with position, which is why an exercise is not the same exercise at a different angle.

rows: Largest in the low arc; deltoid's increases as the arm rises, so the relative demand on the cuff shifts through range
Different muscle contributions, different capsular tension and different functional relevance — both are needed in a programme
Extending the elbow roughly doubles the torque demand of the same hand-held weight
Holding a load at 90° of elevation imposes far greater joint and cuff demand than the same load at 30°

content.body: The loads are larger than residents expect. Glenohumeral joint reaction forces approaching or exceeding body weight are generated during mid-range elevation with modest hand-held loads, because the cuff and deltoid must generate large forces across very short moment arms to balance a long lever.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
This is why the arm's own weight is a real training load — and also a real provocation.
A 4 kg arm held at 90° of elevation is a meaningful demand for a deconditioned tendon. It explains why sustained overhead occupational postures are so provocative, why a hairdresser or an electrician flares at work and not at the gym, and why reducing time at height can be more therapeutic than reducing weight lifted.
It also means unloaded range-of-motion exercise is not a null stimulus in a highly irritable shoulder — supine elevation reduces the demand substantially, which is why it is often the best starting position (11.4).
3.13 Biomechanics V — how the mechanics fail

content.body: The sequence below is the mechanical story of the condition and ties the anatomy to the clinical picture.

1. Tendon capacity falls (age, metabolic, disuse) or load rises
  2. Pain, and reduced capacity to generate compression
  3. Fulcrum degraded → deltoid translates rather than rotates
  4. Compensation: shrugging, early scapular elevation, trunk lean
  5. Altered loading of the cuff and bursa; efficiency falls further
  6. Avoidance → deconditioning → further loss of capacity (the loop)
The loop is the point. Each step reduces capacity further, which is why the condition becomes self-sustaining and why the exit is re-loading, not rest.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Most of what you see on examination is compensation, not primary pathology.
The shrug, the trunk lean, the loss of smooth lowering — these are downstream of a painful, under-capacity tendon. Chasing them as if they were the cause produces a programme of movement-pattern correction that never builds any capacity.
Treat the capacity, and most of the compensation resolves on its own. Retrain movement when it persists after capacity has improved, or when the symptom-modification test says it is contributing now.
3.14 What the anatomy tells you to train

content.body: Collecting all of the above into the prescription it implies:

rows: Include axially loaded and closed-chain work, not only open-chain rotation
External rotation at 0° and at 45–90°, plus genuine internal rotation loading
Internal rotation and belly-press patterns deserve real load, not token resistance
Inferior cuff strength protects against superior migration
Load scaption through range, not just the first 15°
Serratus anterior and lower trapezius work, especially above 90°
Moment arm and demand change with position (3.12)
Progress position deliberately: supine → upright → overhead
Use elbow position as a dosing variable, not an afterthought
Force is delivered from the trunk and legs in overhead tasks
Kinetic chain training for athletes and manual workers
The enthesis does not regenerate after repair (3.3)

content.text: 4. Pathophysiology — how a tendon works, adapts and fails

content.body: This section is longer than most textbooks make it, deliberately. Everything in section 11 is a consequence of what follows. If the dose of exercise you prescribe seems arbitrary, it is because this section has not been read.

content.text: 4.1 The three questions pathophysiology has to answer

content.body: A model of this condition is only adequate if it explains all three of these. The old model explains none of them well.

columns: Why it is a problem for the "pinching" model
rows: Mechanical abrasion should produce surface damage on the bursal side; the commonest partial tears are articular-sided
A mechanical cause should produce pain proportional to the mechanical abnormality; it does not
If the problem were abrasion, loading would be the last thing that works — yet it is the only intervention with durable effect

content.body: The model that answers all three is failed adaptation to load in a tendon whose capacity has fallen.

content.text: 4.2 The old model: extrinsic impingement

content.body:
Neer proposed that the cuff is abraded by the undersurface of the anterior acromion and the coracoacromial ligament, with a progression from bursitis to tendinitis to tear. Bigliani then described three acromial shapes — flat, curved and hooked (type III) — with type III associated with cuff tears.

Three findings undermined this as a causal model:

  1. Acromial shape is at least partly acquired. The hooked appearance is largely a traction enthesophyte at the coracoacromial ligament insertion, developing with age — a consequence of cuff pathology as much as a cause.
  2. Articular-side partial tears are more common than bursal-side tears. Pure extrinsic abrasion from above should produce the opposite.
  3. Removing the acromion does not reliably help. See the surgical evidence in section 13.

What survives of the model. Compression of the cuff and bursa against the coracoacromial arch does occur, can be a source of nociception, and is a reasonable explanation for why certain positions hurt. What does not survive is the claim that acromial geometry causes the disease and that resecting bone cures it.

content.text: 4.3 The intrinsic model

content.body:
The competing tradition holds that the primary event is within the tendon: age-related degeneration, altered cell behaviour, matrix disorganisation and accumulated microdamage, with mechanical contact being a secondary or incidental phenomenon.

Evidence supporting it:

  • Degenerative change is present in asymptomatic tendons and increases steadily with age
  • Articular-sided partial tears predominate — consistent with intrinsic failure under tensile load rather than external abrasion
  • Histology shows degeneration, not inflammation (4.11)
  • Systemic factors — diabetes, smoking, dyslipidaemia, genetics — influence risk, which a purely mechanical external model cannot explain

Its limitation: it does not fully explain why symptoms begin when they do, nor why position-specific pain is so characteristic.

content.text: 4.4 The current integrated model

content.body: Neither extreme is sufficient. The working model combines them, with load as the organising principle.

rows: Age, genetics, metabolic disease, smoking, prior injury, vascular factors
Proteoglycan up, water up, collagen disorganised, type III collagen up, neovessels and nerve ingrowth
Pain (bursa, neural ingrowth, sensitisation) · reduced capacity (structural and material failure) · altered mechanics (compensation, loss of fulcrum)
Which feeds back into the imbalance — the loop

content.body: Modifying factors act throughout: metabolic and vascular health determine the rate of adaptation; psychosocial factors determine pain experience and behaviour; kinematic factors (scapular control, posterior tightness, thoracic posture) alter the distribution of load, though their causal direction is uncertain (6.6).

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Tendinopathy is a capacity problem, not a geometry problem.
Geometry explains which positions hurt. Capacity explains why the shoulder started hurting at all — and capacity is the thing you can change.
4.5 How load becomes adaptation — mechanotransduction

content.body:
This is the mechanism that makes exercise a treatment rather than a coping strategy, and residents should be able to explain it in two minutes to a patient.

The sequence:

  1. Mechanical strain is applied to the tendon during muscle contraction.
  2. Tenocytes sense that strain through integrins linking the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton, through stretch-activated ion channels, and through primary cilia projecting into the matrix.
  3. The mechanical signal is converted into a biochemical one — intracellular calcium flux, release of growth factors including IGF-1 and TGF-beta, and altered gene transcription.
  4. Collagen synthesis increases, predominantly type I, along with matrix proteins and cross-linking enzymes.
  5. Over weeks to months, the tendon's material properties (stiffness, modulus) and sometimes its cross-sectional area change.

The dose–response relationship is an inverted U:

Both ends of that curve are clinically real. Too little load is the patient who rested for three months and is now weaker. Too much, too fast is the patient who returned to decorating at week four. The programme's job is to keep them in the middle of the curve while the middle itself moves rightward.

Three consequences you can act on:

rows: Cells only respond to strain they actually experience
Load must be sufficient. Yellow-band external rotation below the threshold produces no adaptive signal
Both synthesis and degradation rise after loading
Net collagen balance is negative for the first ~24–36 hours and positive thereafter, up to ~72 hours
Immobilisation and rest reduce stiffness and capacity within weeks — rest is an active cause of deterioration

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The negative-then-positive collagen balance is the biological reason for spacing heavy sessions.
After a substantial loading bout, collagen degradation initially exceeds synthesis, and the net balance turns positive only after roughly a day and a half. Repeated heavy loading at less than 24-hour intervals can therefore accumulate net breakdown.
In practice: heavy loading every other day, with lighter work or isometrics on the days between. This is not tradition — it is the reason the classic protocols are three sessions a week rather than seven.
4.6 The mechanical behaviour of tendon

content.body:
Tendon is viscoelastic: its behaviour depends on how much it is loaded and how fast.

The stress–strain curve has three regions worth knowing:

rows: Crimped collagen fibres straightening out. Very compliant
True elastic stretch of aligned collagen. This is where adaptive signalling happens

content.body:
Viscoelastic behaviours you will see clinically:

  • Creep — progressive lengthening under sustained load. Relevant to static overhead or carrying postures, and part of why a long shift is worse than a heavy one.
  • Stress relaxation — force falls when held at constant length. Part of why sustained positions become tolerable and then suddenly provoke.
  • Hysteresis — energy is lost as heat on each loading cycle. Repeated cycling without recovery produces local heating and accumulating microdamage.
  • Rate dependence — a tendon is stiffer when loaded quickly. Fast, high-force tasks (throwing, hammering, catching a falling object) load the tendon in a different mechanical regime from slow lifting, which is why stage 4 of rehabilitation exists.

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Slow heavy load builds the material. Fast load tests it.
Heavy slow resistance generates high strain magnitude held long enough for mechanotransduction. Energy-storage work prepares the tendon for the rate at which real life applies force. A patient who only ever trains slowly is undertrained for a world that includes catching things.
4.7 Why tendon is slower than muscle, and why patients need telling

rows: Early neural gains in 2–4 weeks; hypertrophy 6–12 weeks
High metabolic rate, rich blood supply
Low cell density, slow collagen turnover, modest vascularity

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
This mismatch is the commonest source of patient disappointment, and it is entirely preventable with one sentence at the first appointment.
Patients feel better before they are better. Pain and strength improve on the neural and muscular timeline — weeks — while the tendon's capacity is still on the collagen timeline — months. They then return to full load at week six, flare, and conclude the rehabilitation failed.
Say this at the first visit: "You will feel significantly better in about six weeks. The tendon itself takes about three months. The gap between those two is where people relapse, so we are going to keep loading even after it stops hurting."
4.8 Failed adaptation — what actually happens in the tissue

content.body: This is the mechanistic heart of the chapter. The events below are the maladaptive version of the process described in 4.5.

rows: Load exceeds what the current matrix can tolerate
Tenocytes are mechanically stimulated beyond the adaptive range
Cells become rounded and chondrocyte-like; proliferate
The cell population changes phenotype — it stops behaving like a tendon factory
Water is drawn in; the tendon swells; fibrils are pushed apart
Collagen loses its parallel alignment and crimp
Tensile capacity falls — the tendon is structurally worse at its one job
Type III collagen increases relative to type I
Thinner, less cross-linked fibrils; weaker tissue
New vessels grow in from the paratenon
New nociceptive fibres, substance P and CGRP in the tissue
Pain from tissue that is normally nearly insensate

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Notice what is missing from that list: inflammatory cells, and a tear.
The process is a failed cellular adaptation, not an inflammatory reaction and not a mechanical rupture. That is why anti-inflammatory treatment helps the symptom and not the problem, and why most tendinopathy never progresses to a tear.
It is also why load is the treatment: the cell population that went wrong is the same population that responds to mechanical signalling. You are not repairing tissue — you are re-instructing cells.
4.9 The three kinds of load: tension, compression and shear

content.body: Residents are taught that tendons experience tension. They also experience compression and shear, and the distinction has direct clinical consequences.

columns: Where it occurs in the cuff
rows: Along the line of pull, throughout the tendon
The adaptive stimulus — what you are trying to deliver in rehabilitation
At the enthesis, where tendon wraps the tuberosity, and under the coracoacromial arch in elevation
Drives aggrecan production and fibrocartilage change; poorly tolerated in combination with high tensile load
Between tendon layers and between tendon and bursa, particularly with differential loading of the cuff
Implicated in intrasubstance delamination and partial tears

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Combined compressive and tensile load is the most provocative combination, and it tells you which positions to avoid early.
Sustained end-range elevation and full internal rotation behind the back load the tendon in compression at the same time as it is under tension. In an irritable tendon this combination is the one most likely to flare.
The practical rule for stage 1: load in mid-range, in the scapular plane, below 90°, where tension is available and compression is minimised. Introduce end-range and overhead positions deliberately in stages 3 and 4, once capacity has risen — not because they are dangerous, but because they are expensive.
4.10 The continuum model and why the stage sets your dose

content.body: Cook and Purdam's continuum describes three states, with movement possible in both directions in the earlier stages.

rows: Non-inflammatory proliferative cell response; proteoglycan and water uptake; tendon swells but matrix is intact. Reversible
Younger, acute overload, sudden unaccustomed load, or a direct blow
Reduce load. Then isometrics for symptom control. Do not start heavy loading here
Failed healing; matrix separation, increased vascularity and neural ingrowth
Modify load and begin graded strengthening. The most responsive stage
Cell death, disorganised matrix, neovessels, areas of acellularity. Largely irreversible
Older, long history, often incidental imaging findings
Build capacity in the surrounding normal tissue. Load is still the treatment

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
The doughnut and the hole.
In a degenerative tendon the abnormal area is the hole. It will not be restored. The doughnut — the normal tendon around it — is entirely capable of adapting, and most of the tendon's cross-section is doughnut.
This is why you can honestly tell a 65-year-old with a degenerate supraspinatus that loading will work, even though the degenerate tissue itself will not regenerate. You are not repairing the hole; you are strengthening the ring.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The commonest presentation in a PM&R clinic is "reactive-on-degenerative": an older tendon with established degenerative change that has been acutely overloaded.
Clinically this looks like a long background of niggling discomfort punctuated by a recent sharp deterioration after an identifiable event. It is important because it tells you to treat the reactive component first — settle it with relative rest and isometrics for one to three weeks — and only then begin building capacity in the degenerative substrate.
Going straight to heavy loading in a reactive-on-degenerative tendon is the single commonest reason a well-intentioned programme flares and the patient disengages.
4.11 Histology — why "tendinitis" is the wrong word

content.body:
Tendinopathic tissue shows degenerative, not inflammatory, change:

  • Collagen disorganisation, fibre thinning and loss of crimp
  • Increased ground substance and proteoglycan content, with water uptake
  • Neovascularisation with accompanying neural ingrowth
  • Cellular changes — rounded tenocytes, apoptosis, areas of acellularity
  • Few or no classical inflammatory cells

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
This is why anti-inflammatory logic underperforms. NSAIDs and corticosteroid give short-term symptomatic relief, but they are not treating the dominant pathology, and they do not change the natural history.
Progressive load is the only intervention that addresses the matrix itself — mechanotransduction drives tenocyte activity and collagen synthesis. That is the mechanistic justification for exercise being first-line, and it is worth saying to patients who expect an injection to fix the tendon.
A caveat for accuracy: low-grade inflammatory and neuroimmune signalling is present, particularly in reactive stages and in the bursa, and mediators such as IL-6, prostaglandins and substance P are implicated. "No inflammation at all" overstates it. "Not primarily an inflammatory condition" is right, and is also the accurate thing to tell a patient who asks why the anti-inflammatories only helped for a fortnight.
4.12 Where the pain actually comes from

content.body: Residents are rarely taught this, and it is the key to explaining a confusing presentation. Recall from 3.7 that healthy tendon mid-substance is sparsely innervated — so the pain is mostly coming from somewhere else.

rows: Densely innervated; thickened and sensitised in cuff disease
Pain on compression-type movements, good short-term response to subacromial injection
New nerve fibres growing into tendon with the new vessels
Local mediators (substance P, CGRP, prostaglandins) lowering nociceptor threshold
Marked local tenderness, pain with light load
Widespread pain, poor load–pain relationship, high distress, sleep disruption, long duration
Loading of the insertion, and bone marrow changes at the footprint
Point tenderness at the greater tuberosity

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The load–pain relationship is your most useful diagnostic signal, and it is free.
A tendon problem generally behaves predictably with load: a given activity produces a reasonably reproducible amount of pain, often with a characteristic 24-hour latency — worse the next morning rather than during the activity.
When pain is unpredictable, unrelated to load, widespread, or accompanied by marked distress and sleep disturbance, you are no longer managing a pure capacity problem. The programme must still be loaded, but it needs pacing, education about sensitisation, sleep management and often psychological input — and you should expect progress measured in a different currency.
4.13 Why it hurts at night

content.body: Patients ask this constantly and it is worth being able to answer, because a mechanistic answer is itself reassuring.

rows: Side-lying compresses the bursa and the cuff against the arch
The arm drifts into adduction and internal rotation, a compressive position for the tendon (4.9)
Upright posture allows gravity to distract the joint slightly; lying removes that
Nothing competes with the nociceptive input at 3 a.m.
Cortisol nadir overnight; low-grade mediators less suppressed
Proposed increase in intraosseous and local pressure when recumbent

content.body: What to do with it: night pain is characteristic, not alarming (5.4), and it responds to positioning (10.3) more reliably than to analgesia. It is also worth tracking as an outcome — "how many nights a week does it wake you?" is a sensitive and patient-meaningful measure of progress.

content.text: 4.14 From tendinopathy to tear

content.body:
Not all tendinopathy becomes a tear, but understanding the transition explains the management split.

The mechanics of propagation. Once a defect exists, the load it was carrying is redistributed to the fibres at its edge. Strain concentrates at the tear margin, so the same external load now produces higher local strain there. This is why:

  • Tears tend to propagate rather than heal once they reach a certain size
  • Larger tears enlarge more readily than small ones
  • A tear that unbalances the force couples (3.10) deteriorates functionally much faster than one that does not

Degenerative versus traumatic matters more than size:

rows: Poor; chronic change in the surrounding tendon
Often healthy tendon that failed acutely
Atrophy and fatty infiltration may already be present
Normal at the outset, deteriorating with time

content.label: Memory aid
content.text: Age of the patient, age of the tear, and quality of the muscle decide the pathway. The diameter of the hole decides very little.
4.15 Tear types and what they imply

rows: The deep surface — commonest partial tear
Often degenerative; common in throwers (with internal impingement)
More often symptomatic; associated with compressive load
Within the tendon; often delamination between layers
Often asymptomatic; poorly seen on ultrasound
Superior migration; AHI <7 mm; risk of cuff tear arthropathy

content.text: 4.16 What happens to the muscle after a tear — and why time matters

content.body: This is the single best argument for referring a genuinely traumatic tear early.

rows: Largely irreversible — it does not reverse after repair

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Fatty infiltration is the clock on the operation.
A repairable tear in a patient with Goutallier grade 0–2 has a reasonable chance of healing and functioning. At grade 3–4 the muscle will not recover its contractile capacity even if the tendon is successfully reattached, which is why those tears are often considered irreparable (9.1, 13.2).
This is why "watch and wait" is a reasonable plan for a degenerative tear and a poor one for an acute traumatic tear in a 45-year-old. The tendon can wait; the muscle cannot.
4.17 The bursa — the structure most responsible for the symptoms

content.body: The subacromial–subdeltoid bursa deserves its own mention because it is frequently the dominant pain generator while the tendon is the dominant pathology.

rows: Thickens and becomes fibrotic in chronic cuff disease
Mechanical restriction as well as pain
Explains the reliable short-term effect of a subacromial injection
Does not communicate with the joint normally
Fluid in both compartments implies a full-thickness tear
Treating the bursa alone leaves the capacity problem untouched

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
"Bursitis" is a description of a reaction, not a diagnosis of a cause.
A patient told they have bursitis will reasonably expect an anti-inflammatory solution, and will be puzzled when they are handed a loading programme. The sentence that resolves this: "The lining is irritated because the tendon underneath has been overloaded. Settling the lining helps the pain; building the tendon is what stops it coming back."
5. Clinical presentation — the history as a load investigation
5.1 The typical picture

content.body:
• Lateral deltoid pain, often poorly localised, sometimes radiating to the deltoid insertion but rarely below the elbow
  • Painful arc on elevation, classically 60–120°
  • Night pain, especially lying on the affected side — very common and often the most disabling single feature
  • Difficulty with overhead and behind-the-back activities — a high shelf, washing hair, fastening a bra, reaching a back pocket, a seatbelt
  • Usually gradual onset, often with an identifiable change in load
  • Weakness, if present, is often pain-inhibited rather than structural
  • Stiffness is mild and end-range; global stiffness points elsewhere

content.text: 5.2 The load interview — the questions that actually change the plan

content.body: A good shoulder history is an investigation into the numerator and denominator of 1.2. Ask these, in this order, and notice what each answer is for.

rows: "When did it start, and what were you doing in the month before?"
Looking for the load change, which is usually 2–6 weeks before onset, not the day of onset
Identifies the specific load to modify, and the capacity to rebuild
"What can you not do now that you could do three months ago?"
Converts pain into functional loss, and gives you outcome targets
Becomes the goal list and the discharge criteria
"How much does it take to set it off, and how long does it take to settle?"
"Where exactly, and does it go below the elbow?"
Screening for referred and radicular pain
"Is it worse during the activity or the next morning?"
The classic 24-hour latency of tendon pain
Confirms a load–capacity picture; teaches the patient the monitoring rule
"What have you stopped doing because of it?"
Predicts the capacity you have lost and the psychological work needed
"What do you think is wrong with it?"
Beliefs, previous imaging reports, catastrophic framing
Determines your explanation, which is itself a treatment
"What do you need to get back to?"
Defines the endpoint of the programme and the stage 4 content

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
"What were you doing in the month before it started?" outperforms "what happened?".
Patients report the moment pain appeared. Tendons respond to the preceding accumulation. The painting weekend, the house move, the new gym programme, the holiday with a heavy camera bag, the two weeks covering a colleague's shift — these are three to six weeks upstream of the first symptom and the patient has usually stopped connecting them.
If you ask only "what happened", you will be told "nothing", and you will conclude it came on for no reason. It almost never does.
5.3 Irritability — the single most practically useful assessment

content.body: Irritability describes how easily symptoms are provoked and how long they take to settle. It is not severity, and it is not chronicity. It is the variable that sets your dose.

rows: Pain at rest; night pain every night; provoked by minimal activity (dressing, light reaching); takes hours to settle; active range limited by pain well before passive end-range
Settle first. Isometrics, pain-free range, sleep positioning, activity modification, consider a short NSAID course or an injection as a window. Avoid provocative loading for 1–3 weeks
Pain with moderate activity; some night pain; settles within an hour; active range near passive
Load cautiously but genuinely. Light-to-moderate isotonic loading through tolerable range, 2–3 sets, progress every 1–2 weeks
Pain only with heavy or sustained load; no night pain; settles quickly; full range
Load properly. Heavy slow resistance, higher loads, add range, add speed. Underdosing is now the main risk

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Irritability sets the dose. Diagnosis sets the direction.
Two patients with identical imaging get different programmes if their irritability differs. The diagnosis tells you to load the cuff; irritability tells you how much, starting today.
Reassess it at every visit — it is dynamic, and the programme should move with it.
5.4 Features that point away from simple tendinopathy

rows: Global loss of passive range, external rotation lost first
Acute severe pain, often sleepless, markedly restricted, disproportionate
Neurological — suprascapular neuropathy, C5 radiculopathy, neuralgic amyotrophy, motor neuron disease
Pain below the elbow, dermatomal sensory change
Systemic features, rest pain unrelieved by position, weight loss

content.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content.text:
Pain referred below the elbow is not the rotator cuff. Think cervical radiculopathy, peripheral nerve or referred visceral pain.
Night pain alone is not a red flag — it is characteristic of cuff pathology and is one of the commonest presenting complaints. Night pain with constitutional symptoms, a cancer history, or pain that is completely unaffected by position and movement is.
5.5 The psychosocial screen you should do every time

content.body: The 2025 clinical practice guideline recommends identifying personal, clinical, psychosocial and work-related prognostic factors. In practice this is three questions and takes a minute.

rows: "How do you expect this to turn out?"
Recovery expectation — one of the stronger single predictors of outcome
Spend time on explanation; a pessimistic expectation is modifiable and worth modifying
"How is it affecting your sleep and your mood?"
Sleep disruption and distress, which amplify pain and impair tissue adaptation
Address sleep positioning actively; consider mood and refer if indicated
"Is there anything about work that makes this complicated?"
Job demands, dissatisfaction, compensation context, fear of job loss
Early occupational health involvement; a realistic graded return plan

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Do not file psychosocial factors under "not my problem".
Low expectation of recovery, fear-avoidance, distress and an adversarial compensation context are more predictive of outcome than tear size. They are also partly modifiable — by explanation, by graded exposure, by achievable early wins in the programme, and by not telling a patient their tendon is worn out.
The consultation is not the preamble to the treatment. In this condition it is a substantial part of it.
6. Examination — what each finding changes

content.body: An examination that does not change your plan was a waste of the patient's afternoon. For each element below, the final column is the point.

content.text: 6.1 The structured sequence

rows: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossa wasting, deltoid bulk, scapular resting position, biceps contour (Popeye sign)
Wasting out of proportion to pain → think neurological or chronic massive tear
Can change the diagnosis completely. Never skip
Painful arc, scapulohumeral rhythm, shrug sign, quality of lowering
Identifies the arc to work in and the compensations to retrain
Identifies the structural question and gives your baseline numbers
The common companions; changes injection target
Resting position, dynamic control, assistance/retraction tests
Decides whether scapular work belongs in the programme

content.text: 6.2 Range of motion — measure it, do not eyeball it

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
The 2025 rotator cuff tendinopathy clinical practice guideline grades this A: measure shoulder range with an inclinometer, goniometer or validated smartphone app rather than visual estimation. Scapular range measures are not recommended — their reliability does not support clinical use.
The practical reason: you need a number you can re-measure in six weeks. "Nearly full" is not a number, and visual estimation drifts in the direction you hope.
Interpretation of the active–passive relationship:

rows: Pain inhibition or structural cuff failure — distinguish with lag signs
Active and passive equally limited, ER lost first
Active full but painful in an arc
Classic rotator cuff related shoulder pain

content.text: 6.3 Strength testing — use a dynamometer and record the numbers

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
The same guideline grades this A: use a handheld dynamometer for isometric shoulder strength. Manual muscle testing is not recommended — it is insensitive to the deficits that matter, and nearly everyone grades 5/5 against a motivated examiner.
What to record, every time:

rows: The most consistently affected and the most prognostic

content.body:
Benchmarks worth knowing:

  • ER:IR ratio of roughly 0.65–0.75 is commonly cited as normal. A ratio well below this suggests a posterior cuff deficit worth targeting.
  • Limb symmetry index >90% is a reasonable return-to-sport and return-to-heavy-work criterion for ER and IR strength.
  • Absolute values matter less than the change in the same patient measured the same way.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Dynamometry converts rehabilitation from an opinion into a measurement.
Three numbers at baseline — ER, IR, scaption — repeated at six and twelve weeks, tell you whether your programme is working, tell the patient their shoulder is objectively stronger even on a day it hurts, and give you something concrete for the discharge letter.
It is also the only honest way to answer "has physiotherapy failed?". A patient whose ER strength has not changed in eight weeks has not failed rehabilitation — they have failed to be adequately loaded.
6.4 Tendon-specific strength tests

rows: Arm at 90° in the scapular plane, thumb up; resist downward force. Comparable accuracy with less pain provocation than empty can
Resisted external rotation at the side; external rotation lag sign
Lag sign: passively place at near-maximal ER; a lag on release suggests a tear
Arm at 90° abduction, 90° elbow flexion; inability to externally rotate
Lift-off requires internal rotation range; belly press is usable when it is restricted. Bear hug is sensitive for upper-third tears

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Lag signs are more useful than pain-provocation tests.
A painful test tells you a structure is sensitised. A lag sign — the inability to hold a passively placed position — tells you the tendon cannot transmit force, which points toward a structural tear.
The external rotation lag sign and the drop arm sign have better specificity than Neer or Hawkins-Kennedy, and they change management more often — because they are the findings that move a patient from the rehabilitation pathway to a surgical conversation.
6.5 Provocation tests — and their real diagnostic value

columns: What it was said to show
rows: Passive forward flexion in internal rotation
Inability to lower the arm smoothly from abduction

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
Individually, these tests perform poorly. Systematic reviews consistently find that no single physical examination test reliably diagnoses rotator cuff pathology or distinguishes it from other shoulder conditions.
The 2025 clinical practice guideline makes a usefully specific recommendation (grade B): use the painful arc to help confirm rotator cuff tendinopathy and the Hawkins-Kennedy test to help rule it out — while explicitly stating that clinicians should not rely on test results alone for diagnosis.
In likelihood-ratio language: the painful arc is the better rule-in test of the group; a negative Hawkins-Kennedy is a reasonable rule-out. Everything else is confirmation of a story you already have.
The honest position to teach: the examination's main value is in excluding other diagnoses — adhesive capsulitis by passive range, radiculopathy by the cervical screen, instability by apprehension, neurological causes by the pattern of weakness — rather than in confirming cuff pathology, which the history and the pattern of loss already suggest.

content.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content.text:
Do not tell a patient that a positive Hawkins test means their tendon is being pinched.
It does not mean that. It means a provocative compressive position hurts, which is true in a large number of shoulder conditions and in some asymptomatic people.
The sentence costs you nothing to say and can cost the patient a year of protective behaviour, because they will now avoid every position that resembles the test.
6.6 Scapular assessment — useful, with a caveat

content.body: Look at resting position (anterior tilt, downward rotation, winging), dynamic control during elevation and especially during lowering (where control fails first), and perform the scapular assistance test (manually assisting upward rotation and posterior tilt during elevation) and the scapular retraction test (manually stabilising in retraction during strength testing).

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
Scapular dyskinesis is common in asymptomatic people, particularly overhead athletes, and its association with shoulder pain is weaker than commonly taught. Causal direction is unclear: altered scapular motion may be a consequence of pain rather than its cause. Scapular range measures are not recommended for clinical use.
It is better understood as a potential contributing factor and a modifiable treatment target than as a diagnosis or a cause.
The useful distinction: static observation of scapular position has poor reliability and limited meaning. Symptom modification does have meaning. If assisting the scapula changes the patient's pain now, you have found something worth training. If it does not, do not build the programme around it.
6.7 Symptom modification — turning examination into prescription

content.body:
This is the most directly useful thing you will do in the physical examination, and it is frequently omitted.

The method: find a movement that reproduces the patient's pain, then apply a modification and immediately retest. If pain reduces meaningfully, that modification becomes the starting point of the exercise programme.

rows: Scapular control work belongs in the programme
Manually stabilise retracted during strength test
Train scapular setting and posterior chain
Scaption instead of pure abduction, or thumb-up instead of thumb-down
Prescribe in the tolerated plane and progress toward the provocative one
Work below 90° rather than through the painful arc
Sitting tall, or elevation performed in extension

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The best first exercise is the modification that made them comfortable in clinic.
Patients leave with a programme they have already succeeded at once, in front of you, which does more for adherence than any explanation. It also means your prescription is individualised by a test rather than by a protocol.
Write it down in the terms you used: "scaption to 70°, thumb up, 1 kg, with the scapula set — this was pain-free today."
6.8 Turning the examination into a plan

rows: Painful arc, full passive range, no lag
Positive lag sign, weakness disproportionate to pain
Image; consider surgical opinion; load in the meantime
Serratus and lower trapezius work, early and prominent
Posterior tightness, reduced cross-body and IR at 90°
Add posterior mobility; do not make it the whole plan
Prioritise ER loading at 0° and at 45–90°
Pain unchanged by every modification, widespread, high distress

Thoracic mobility, but as an adjunct

content.text: 7. Differential diagnosis
7.1 The full list

rows: Global passive restriction, external rotation lost first; progresses through painful → stiff → thawing phases; strongly associated with diabetes
Passive restriction with crepitus; radiographic change
Pain localised to the AC joint; positive cross-body adduction; pain at end-range elevation. Near-universal degeneration after 40 — needs tenderness + provocative test + response to block
Acute severe pain, often disproportionate; calcification on radiograph or ultrasound; distinct treatment pathway
Anterior pain in the bicipital groove; often coexists with cuff disease
Pain below the elbow, dermatomal sensory change, positive Spurling's, neurological signs
Isolated infraspinatus wasting with weak external rotation; consider spinoglenoid cyst
Severe pain preceding patchy weakness; respects no single nerve; often post-viral or post-immunisation
Apprehension, clunking, younger patient, often sport-related
