content.text: 7.2 A five-move triage for any shoulder

content.body: Residents find a sequence more useful than a list. These five moves sort almost every shoulder in under five minutes.

rows: Is the pain coming from the shoulder at all?
Is this a stiff shoulder or a painful one?
Globally stiff → adhesive capsulitis or OA
Weakness without pain, or non-myotomal pattern → neurological workup
Clear load change + painful arc → rotator cuff related shoulder pain

content.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content.text:
The cervical spine is the single most commonly missed cause of "shoulder pain." C5 radiculopathy mimics cuff disease closely, and often presents without neck pain.
Screen the neck in every shoulder presentation. It takes thirty seconds and it is the error most likely to appear in a complaint letter.
8. Investigations
8.1 When to image — and why "not yet" is a defensible answer

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
The 2025 clinical practice guideline is explicit: do not order imaging to confirm rotator cuff tendinopathy during initial management, and consider imaging if symptoms do not improve within 12 weeks of appropriate non-surgical care. When imaging is needed, it recommends prioritising diagnostic ultrasound, which has accuracy similar to MRI at lower cost, and explicitly recommends explaining the value and limits of imaging to the patient.
Image earlier when:
  • There is trauma with suspicion of an acute tear
  • There is significant weakness or a positive lag sign
  • Symptoms fail to improve after an adequate trial of rehabilitation
  • Surgery is being considered
  • Red flags are present

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The reason to delay imaging is not cost. It is that a scan changes the patient's beliefs more than it changes your management.
A report containing "tear", "degeneration" and "bursitis" in a 60-year-old describes findings present in a large proportion of pain-free people of the same age. But the patient now has a structural explanation for their pain, a reason to protect the arm, and a reason to doubt a loading programme.
If you are going to image, pre-frame the result: "We will almost certainly see some age-related change in the tendon. That is expected and it does not change the plan — I am looking specifically for a tear that would alter what we do."
8.2 Modalities

rows: First-line structural film. AP, scapular Y, axillary. Look for acromiohumeral interval, calcific deposits, AC and glenohumeral degeneration, greater tuberosity change, os acromiale

The physiatrist's tool. Comparable accuracy to MRI for full-thickness tears in experienced hands; dynamic assessment; guides injection; immediate and patient-facing; recommended first in the 2025 guideline
Best for intrasubstance pathology, labrum, muscle quality. Fatty infiltration (Goutallier) and muscle atrophy predict repairability and outcome
Higher sensitivity for partial-thickness and labral tears

content.text: 8.3 Ultrasound technique

content.label: Imaging and procedures
content.text:
Standard diagnostic sequence:
  1. Long head of biceps in short axis — the anchoring landmark; then long axis
  2. Subscapularis in external rotation — long and short axis
  3. Supraspinatus — modified Crass position (hand in back pocket, elbow back)
  4. Infraspinatus and teres minor — posterior
  5. Dynamic assessment — bursal bunching on elevation, subscapularis sliding
  6. AC joint and posterior glenohumeral joint
Beware anisotropy — the commonest cause of a false-positive tear. Confirm any suspected lesion in two planes, and keep the probe perpendicular.
Findings and their weight: hypoechoic clefts with a volume defect and reproducible in two planes are meaningful; isolated hypoechogenicity, heterogeneity, and small bursal fluid are extremely common and often incidental.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
Age-stratified prevalence of asymptomatic cuff abnormality is the number every resident should know.
Systematic review data show rotator cuff abnormalities in asymptomatic shoulders rising from roughly 10% in those under 20 to over 60% in those aged 80 and above. Full-thickness tears specifically are less common but follow the same trajectory, and asymptomatic tears are frequently bilateral.
So a tear on a scan does not establish the cause of the pain. Report the finding, but interpret it against the clinical picture — and be careful how you word it. "Age-related change in the tendon" conveys the same fact as "a tear" without implying a structure that has broken and needs fixing.
8.4 How to word a report or explain one

rows: "There is some age-related thinning in the tendon, which is common at your age and is not the reason we're choosing treatment"
"The tendon has changed with time, like grey hair — the job now is to build its strength"
"You have bone spurs pinching the tendon"
"The shape of the bone varies between people and changes with age; it isn't what decides your outcome"
"The lining is irritated because the tendon has been overloaded"
Links the finding to the mechanism you are treating

content.text: 9. Classification and staging
9.1 Why formal staging matters less than you would expect

content.body:
Several classification systems exist — Neer's stages (I oedema, II fibrosis, III tear), Ellman for partial tears by depth, Cofield by tear size, Patte by retraction, Goutallier for fatty infiltration.

Of these, the two that genuinely change management are:

  • Goutallier grade of fatty infiltration — grade 3–4 predicts poor repair outcome and is often considered irreparable
  • Patte retraction stage, for the same reason

Tear size alone predicts outcome poorly. Muscle quality predicts it well. Fatty infiltration and atrophy are largely irreversible, which is the real argument for referring a genuinely traumatic tear early rather than watching it.

content.text: 9.2 The practical classification — the one that changes your plan

rows: Pain and dysfunction; no lag sign; imaging shows tendinosis ± bursal change
Older patient, gradual onset, preserved active range
Clear injury, immediate weakness, positive lag sign, younger patient
Rehabilitation focused on the anterior deltoid programme (13.5); surgical options are reconstructive

content.text: 9.3 Staging by continuum position — what sets your starting dose

content.body: Cross-reference this with 4.10 and 5.3. This is the staging that determines the first three weeks of the programme.

rows: Recent clear overload, high irritability, often swollen-feeling and acutely painful tendon
Weeks-to-months history, moderate irritability, pain predictable with load
Begin isotonic loading now, progress every 1–2 weeks
Long history, low irritability, pain only with heavy or sustained load
Load heavily and progressively. The main error here is underdosing

content.text: 10. Management principles — what you are actually trying to change
10.1 The four targets

content.body: Before any specific intervention, be clear what you are aiming at. Every treatment in sections 11 and 12 serves one of these, and anything that serves none of them should be dropped.

rows: Predicts outcome; determines adherence and behaviour
The proximate cause and the thing you can change today
Activity modification, ergonomics, sleep positioning, pacing
The actual treatment; the only thing that changes the tendon
Determines how fast capacity can rise
Glycaemic control, smoking, sleep, weight, mood

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Explain, unload, reload, and fix the background.
A plan that does not touch all four is incomplete, and the one most often skipped is the first.
10.2 Education — the intervention that costs nothing and predicts outcome

content.body:
What to explain, in the patient's words:

  • The tendon is not torn by the pain and is not fragile
  • Pain does not equal damage — this is a capacity problem
  • Imaging findings are common with age and do not dictate the outcome
  • The goal is to build capacity, which takes months, not weeks
  • Some discomfort during loading is acceptable and expected (10.4)
  • Rest makes it worse in the medium term, because it lowers capacity further

Three explanations that work in clinic:

content.label: The capacity line
content.text: "Think of your tendon as having a line — how much it can handle. Life has been asking for more than the line. We can lower the ask for a few weeks, but the real job is to raise the line, and that's what the exercises do."

content.label: The grey-hair line, for imaging
content.text: "The scan shows the tendon has changed with age. So has mine. These changes are on the scans of plenty of people with no pain at all — which is why the scan doesn't decide the treatment."

content.label: The tooth-brushing line, for adherence
content.text: "This isn't a course of treatment that finishes. It's more like brushing your teeth — twice a week for the next few months, and then whatever keeps it comfortable."

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Ask what they believe before you explain anything.
A patient who believes their tendon is "worn out and bone on bone" needs a different conversation from one who thinks they simply pulled something. If you deliver your standard explanation without knowing which you are facing, half of your patients hear reassurance and the other half hear that you did not understand how bad it is.
10.3 Load management — relative rest, and the three levers

content.body:
This is the intervention most often skipped and most often decisive. It is also where residents make opposite errors in equal numbers.

The three levers you can pull in week one:

rows: Lighter toolbag, two trips instead of one, smaller jug
Total repetitions and recovery between bouts
Break the decorating into 20-minute blocks; alternate overhead and bench-height tasks
Where in range and how long it is held
Work below shoulder height where possible; use a step instead of reaching; change the bench or monitor height

content.body:
What not to do:

  • Do not immobilise. A sling for cuff tendinopathy reduces capacity and risks a stiff shoulder on top of a painful one.
  • Do not recommend complete rest "until it settles". It will settle, the capacity will be lower, and the first return to normal activity will flare it.
  • Do not change everything at once. Change the one or two loads the history identified, so you can tell what worked.

Sleep, specifically. Night pain is often the most disabling symptom and is worth a dedicated two minutes:

  • Lie on the unaffected side with the affected arm supported on a pillow in front, slightly flexed and internally rotated
  • Or lie supine with a small towel under the elbow, so the arm is not hanging into extension
  • Avoid sleeping with the arm overhead
  • Treat persistent sleep disruption actively — poor sleep amplifies pain and impairs tissue adaptation

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Relative rest, not rest. The commonest error in the first six weeks is complete avoidance, which lowers capacity and makes the eventual return to load harder.
The second commonest error is the exact opposite — continuing the provocative load unchanged while adding exercises on top, and expecting the exercises to win. They will not. You cannot out-train a load you have not modified.
10.4 Pain during exercise — the rule you give every patient

content.body:
Patients will ask "should it hurt?". You need one answer, every time, and it needs to be specific enough to act on.

The monitoring model:

rows: Pain up to about 4–5/10 is acceptable, provided it is the familiar pain and not sharp or new
Should not be markedly worse than before starting
Must settle back to baseline. This is the critical rule
Stiffness and pain should not be progressively worse from week to week
Reduce load by roughly 20–30%, or reduce range or volume, and progress again from there

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
Does allowing pain during exercise improve outcomes?
Trials comparing painful with pain-free exercise protocols, including in rotator cuff related shoulder pain, show at most small short-term differences, with no clear long-term superiority of either approach. A reasonable reading: permitting moderate, monitored pain is safe and allows faster loading, but it is not itself therapeutic, and insisting on it is not supported.
The practical value of the rule is permission and a boundary. It stops the patient who abandons the programme at the first twinge, and it stops the patient who trains into a flare every session.

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Up to 5 during, back to baseline by tomorrow.
If both are true, the dose was right. If the second is false, the dose was too high — regardless of what the first said.
11. The loading programme

content.body: This section is the chapter's centre of gravity. Everything before it was preparation.

content.text: 11.1 What the evidence does and does not say

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
The evidence is strong for exercise and weak for any specific protocol.
The 2025 clinical practice guideline gives its highest grade (A) to prescribing an active rehabilitation exercise programme as initial treatment, stating it may include motor control and/or resistance training with various loads — notably without specifying the dose, because the trial evidence does not support specifying it.
Systematic reviews consistently find that no particular exercise type — eccentric, concentric, isometric, heavy slow resistance — is clearly superior for rotator cuff related shoulder pain. The comparison between higher and lower dose exercise shows possible benefit for function with higher doses, with low-certainty evidence and no clear effect on pain.
What this means for you. You are not choosing between protocols with different efficacy. You are applying the principles of tissue adaptation to an individual, and the specific exercises matter far less than the following five things:

rows: It is progressive and loaded, not just range-of-motion work
It is adequately dosed and continued long enough
It is individualised by irritability and by target load
Dose must match the tissue state and the goal
It is supervised at least initially, with progression reviewed
The main failure mode is a programme that never progresses
The patient understands why they are doing it
Adherence over months requires a rationale, not a handout

content.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content.text:
"Failed physiotherapy" is usually a failed dose, not a failed treatment.
Before accepting that conservative management has failed, ask three questions: What load were they actually lifting? How often? And did it ever increase?
Four sessions of pendulums and a yellow band over six weeks is not a trial of rehabilitation. It is a reason to start one.
11.2 The dose variables you are prescribing

content.body: Every exercise prescription is a set of choices along these axes. Write them down; "cuff exercises, 3 sets of 10" is not a prescription.

rows: Isometric at a % of maximum, or isotonic at an RM-based load
2–4 sessions per week for heavy work
Slow (≈3 s each way) for capacity building
Which arc the work is done in
Start where it is tolerable, progress toward the provocative arc
Degrees of elevation, plane, lever length
Progress from short lever and low elevation to long lever and overhead

content.label: Memory aid
content.text:
Load, volume, frequency, tempo, range, position.
When a programme stalls, change one of these — not all six. When a programme flares, reduce one — usually load or range — rather than stopping entirely.
11.3 Choosing the starting point

rows: Stage 2 at a conservative load, with isometrics retained for pain control
Stage 2 at a genuine load, progressing quickly to stage 3

content.text: 11.4 Stage 1 — settle and activate

content.body:
Goal: reduce irritability, maintain range, restore basic control, and establish the habit of daily engagement. Typical duration: 1–3 weeks. Do not park a patient here for two months.

Content:

rows: 5 × 30–45 s holds at roughly 60–70% of maximum, 1–2 min rest, 1–2 × daily. Typically external rotation at 0°, with the arm at the side
Loads the tendon without movement through a provocative arc; tolerable at high irritability
Through tolerable range, several times daily; supine elevation is often best tolerated
Gentle upward rotation and posterior tilt in sitting and supine
Restores the positioning element without loading the cuff
Reduces the total load while capacity is low

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
Isometrics for analgesia — a claim that has been downgraded.
An influential 2015 trial in patellar tendinopathy reported substantial immediate pain relief after isometric holds, and this became widely taught. Subsequent studies have largely failed to replicate it, including in Achilles tendinopathy, and a meta-analysis found isometric exercise no better than other forms of exercise for tendon pain.
The defensible position: isometrics are a well-tolerated way to load a highly irritable tendon, and many individual patients do report relief. They are not a specially analgesic modality, and they are not a destination — they are a means of loading something you cannot yet move through range.
If a patient finds them analgesic, use them. If not, move on to stage 2 sooner.
11.5 Stage 2 — build capacity

content.body:
This is the stage that actually treats the condition, and it is where most programmes are underdosed.

Goal: progressively increase the load the cuff and scapular muscles can tolerate. Typical duration: 6–12 weeks, often longer.

The core prescription:

rows: Heavy slow resistance — controlled concentric and eccentric
Start around a 12–15 repetition maximum; progress toward 6–8 RM over weeks
3–4 sets, repetitions falling as load rises (15 → 12 → 10 → 8 → 6)
2–3 heavy sessions per week, on non-consecutive days
Increase load when the top of the rep range is completed with good control and the 24-hour rule is satisfied — typically every 1–2 weeks

content.body:
Why heavy and slow. High load generates the strain magnitude required for mechanotransduction (4.5–4.6). Slow tempo increases time under tension and keeps the strain within the controlled, elastic part of the curve instead of relying on momentum. Alternate-day frequency respects the collagen synthesis timeline.

The core exercises and what each is for:

rows: External rotation at 0° (band or cable, towel under arm)
The foundation. Must become genuinely heavy, not a warm-up
Posterior cuff in a functional position
Progress to this; the moment arm and demand differ from 0°
Frequently neglected; the largest cuff muscle deserves real load
Progress range as tolerance allows; thumb up
Builds the base for overhead work
Prone Y / side-lying ER / prone horizontal abduction with ER
High activation with low upper-trapezius dominance
Loaded carries, wall press, quadruped weight shift
Closed-chain and axial loading — the 3.9 rationale

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The commonest failure of a cuff programme is that the load never changes.
A patient doing three sets of fifteen with a yellow band in week two should not still be doing three sets of fifteen with a yellow band in week eight. If they are, the programme is maintenance, not treatment.
At every review, ask: what are you lifting now, and what were you lifting last time? If the answer is the same, fix that before considering anything else.
11.6 Stage 3 — range, position and complexity

content.body: Goal: extend capacity into the ranges and positions the patient actually needs, especially overhead. Begin when stage 2 loading is tolerated through available range with controlled 24-hour responses.

rows: Scaption to 120° then full; incline and overhead press patterns
Standing rather than supported; straight-arm rather than bent
Diagonal patterns, overhead carries, landmine press progressing to overhead press
Higher repetitions at sustained overhead positions, for workers who hold rather than lift
Single-arm carries and presses, reflecting real tasks

content.text: 11.7 Stage 4 — energy storage, speed and sport

content.body:
Who needs it: overhead athletes, throwers, racket and combat sports, manual workers who apply force quickly (hammering, scaffolding, catching, lifting awkward loads), and anyone whose target task involves rapid or unpredictable loading.

Who does not: a 70-year-old whose goal is a kitchen shelf. For them, stage 3 is the finish line.

rows: Chest-pass and overhead throws with a medicine ball, wall dribbles, rapid band ER
Tendon is rate-dependent (4.6); it must be prepared for fast force application
Catching a weighted ball overhead; controlled fast lowering
Deceleration is where the cuff fails in throwing
Structured interval throwing programme; graded serving or spiking volume
Reintroduces the exact provocative load under control
Rotational medicine-ball work from the hips; trunk and single-leg strength
In overhead throwing a large majority of the energy delivered to the hand originates in the legs and trunk

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
For throwers and overhead workers, the shoulder is the last link, not the problem.
If the hips, trunk and scapula do not deliver and position force, the cuff absorbs the shortfall every repetition. A thrower rehabilitated only at the shoulder returns to the same kinematics that overloaded it, and relapses.
Stage 4 is where you earn the return to sport. Skipping it is why so many throwers get better in clinic and worse on the field.
11.8 Progression and regression — explicit rules

content.body:
Residents are rarely given decision rules, so they progress by instinct or not at all. Use these.

Progress when all of the following are true:

  • The patient completes the top of the prescribed rep range with controlled tempo and no compensation
  • Pain during exercise is ≤4–5/10 and familiar
  • Symptoms return to baseline within 24 hours
  • Morning stiffness is not increasing week on week

How to progress — one variable at a time, in this order:

  1. Load (the default, and the one most often neglected)
  2. Range (further into elevation, or into the previously provocative arc)
  3. Position (greater abduction, longer lever, less support)
  4. Speed (only in stage 4)

Regress when:

  • Symptoms do not settle within 24 hours
  • Morning pain or stiffness is worse week on week
  • The patient compensates (shrugging, trunk lean, holding breath) to complete reps
  • A flare occurs — reduce load by 20–30% and rebuild, rather than stopping

content.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content.text:
Do not respond to a flare by stopping the programme.
A flare means the dose exceeded current capacity. The correct response is a smaller dose, not no dose. Stopping teaches the patient that loading is dangerous, costs the capacity already gained, and usually means starting again two weeks later from a lower baseline.
Tell them this in advance, at the first appointment, so that the inevitable bad week does not end the treatment.
11.9 The prescription sheet

content.body: What a written programme should contain. Anything less is a suggestion.

rows: Cable external rotation, arm at side, towel under elbow
Up to 5/10 during; back to normal by the next morning
When 4 × 12 is comfortable, increase by 1 kg

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Ask the patient to record the load. A simple note on a phone — date, exercise, weight, reps — does three things: it makes progression visible when pain is not yet improving, it tells you at review whether the dose actually increased, and it converts an abstract instruction into a measurable behaviour.
It is also the quickest way to find out that the "12-week trial of physiotherapy" involved the same green band throughout.
11.10 Adherence — the real determinant of outcome

content.body: A perfect programme performed twice is worse than a mediocre one performed for three months.

rows: Three to four exercises maximum. A programme of eight will not be done
Use dynamometry and the load log; show the numbers
Explain mechanotransduction in one sentence: "load is the signal that tells the tendon to rebuild"
Give the 24-hour rule explicitly, and warn about flares in advance
Agree a minimum effective dose for bad weeks — one heavy session rather than none
Explain the 4.5 mismatch: feeling better precedes being better. Continue to 12 weeks and beyond

Mobility work buys you a better position to load in. It is not the treatment — loading is.
The test is simple: if you removed the stretch from the programme but kept the loading, would the patient still get better? Usually yes. Reverse it, and usually no.

Steps 2 and 4 account for most "failures".
In the majority of patients referred as "failed conservative management", either the exercise dose never progressed or the provocative load was never modified. Both are correctable in one appointment, and both are more productive than a third injection.

content.body: B. Low irritability, degenerative — 67-year-old with a small degenerative full-thickness supraspinatus tear, wants to garden and swim

Stage 4: medicine-ball overhead throws, rapid-rate band work, deceleration control, graded hitting volume by count

content.label: Memory aid
content.text: If it does not change load, change capacity, or change beliefs, it is an adjunct — and adjuncts buy time rather than outcomes.
12.2 Corticosteroid injection

content.body:
What it does: reliable short-term pain relief, typically most marked over the first 6–8 weeks.

What it does not do: improve outcomes beyond the short term compared with exercise, or change the natural history of the tendon.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
The 2025 guideline position is worth quoting in both halves: corticosteroid injection may be recommended to reduce pain and short-term disability (grade B), and is not recommended as a first-line treatment (grade C). Ultrasound guidance for subacromial injection is recommended where available (grade B).
That pairing is the whole clinical message: it works, briefly, and it belongs after or alongside a loading programme rather than instead of one.

rows: Blind subacromial injection reaches the target roughly 50–70% of the time; ultrasound guidance exceeds 90%
Limit the number; repeated injections are associated with worse tendon outcomes
Injection within approximately 3 months of rotator cuff repair is associated with higher re-tear and revision rates
Warn about transient hyperglycaemia, which can be marked and last several days
Give a loading plan for the analgesic window, and advise avoiding heavy provocative load for the first week or two

content.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content.text:
Never inject into the tendon itself, and be cautious about repeated injections in a patient you intend to load heavily. Corticosteroid has documented adverse effects on tenocyte function and collagen synthesis.
The defensible use of injection is as a window, not a treatment: it reduces pain enough to let the patient engage with the loading programme. Give it with a rehabilitation plan attached, not instead of one — and if you are giving a third injection to the same shoulder, the plan is what has failed, not the tendon.
12.3 Other injectables

rows: Guideline grades D/F — may be used, not first-line. Evidence remains inconsistent with heterogeneous preparations. Reasonable to discuss with honest uncertainty, including cost
Grades D/F — may be used for short- and medium-term pain, not first-line

content.label: Imaging and procedures
content.text:
Practical points for an ultrasound-guided subacromial injection:
  • Position: seated, arm in slight internal rotation and extension (modified Crass opens the lateral subacromial window), or lateral decubitus
  • Approach: lateral, in-plane, probe in the coronal oblique plane over the greater tuberosity
  • Confirm the needle tip in the bursa, between the deltoid and the supraspinatus tendon — injectate should spread along the bursa, not distend the tendon
  • If the injectate does not flow freely and the tendon fibres separate, you are in the tendon — stop and reposition
  • Document the target, the drug and volume, the guidance used, and the rehabilitation plan that follows
13. Surgery and post-operative rehabilitation
13.1 Subacromial decompression — the operation built on the old model

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
Two landmark placebo-controlled trials changed practice.
CSAW (Beard et al., Lancet 2018) randomised patients to arthroscopic subacromial decompression, investigational arthroscopy without decompression (placebo surgery), or no treatment. Decompression produced no clinically important benefit over placebo surgery.
FIMPACT (Paavola et al., BMJ 2018) compared decompression, diagnostic arthroscopy alone, and exercise, with similar results.
The implication: improvement after decompression is largely attributable to natural history, the rehabilitation that follows, and placebo effect. Routine subacromial decompression for rotator cuff related shoulder pain is no longer supported, and several national guidelines now advise against it.
How to use this in clinic. It is not an argument to refuse referral; it is an argument for sequencing. A patient who has had a genuine, progressive, adequately dosed loading programme and remains disabled is a reasonable surgical discussion. A patient who has had four sessions of pendulums is not — and telling them so, with the evidence, is more useful than a referral.
13.2 Rotator cuff repair — a different question

content.body:
Reasonable indications:

  • Acute traumatic full-thickness tear, especially in a younger or active patient — refer early, as delay allows retraction and fatty infiltration that repair does not reverse
  • Significant functional deficit from a repairable tear after a genuine rehabilitation trial
  • Progressive tear enlargement with worsening function

Less favourable:

  • Goutallier grade 3–4 fatty infiltration — often irreparable
  • Massive retracted tears with established superior migration
  • Poorly controlled diabetes, heavy smoking — both predict poorer healing
  • Age alone is a weak criterion; tissue quality and demand matter more

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
For non-traumatic cuff disease, exercise performs comparably to surgery in trials with medium-term follow-up, including for many degenerative full-thickness tears, and systematic reviews report comparable improvements in quality of life, disability and pain even for large-to-massive degenerative tears managed with structured exercise.
Exercise is cheaper, carries no operative risk, and does not preclude later surgery. That last point is the one to tell an anxious patient: choosing rehabilitation first does not close a door.
13.3 The healing biology that dictates the protocol

content.body: Residents follow post-operative protocols without knowing why the phases exist. Here is the biology.

rows: Haematoma, cytokine release, cell recruitment. The repair is held only by suture fixation
Protect absolutely. Sling; passive motion only, in safe arcs
Fibrovascular scar forms at the tendon–bone interface. Biological strength is at its lowest in the first 2–3 weeks, as fixation weakens before scar matures
The highest-risk window for re-tear. No active elevation; no resisted work
Collagen aligns along lines of stress; interface strength rises
Active-assisted → active motion; gentle isometrics late in this phase
Continued remodelling; tissue never fully recovers the native enthesis
Progressive strengthening from ~12 weeks; power and sport later

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The repaired enthesis does not regenerate — it scars.
The native insertion is a graded four-zone transition from tendon to fibrocartilage to mineralised fibrocartilage to bone. Repair produces fibrovascular scar instead, which is weaker. That is why re-tear rates are substantial — roughly 10–20% for small tears and far higher, up to 40% and beyond, for massive tears — and why strengthening is deferred to around three months.
Tell the patient this early. It reframes the sling from an inconvenience into the thing protecting their operation.
13.4 A typical post-operative sequence

content.body: Follow the operating surgeon's protocol. The table below is the common shape, not a substitute for it — and it varies substantially with tear size, tissue quality, and whether subscapularis was repaired.

rows: Protect repair, prevent stiffness, control pain
Sling (often abduction pillow for larger repairs); passive forward elevation and ER within surgeon's limits; elbow, wrist, hand; scapular setting; cryotherapy
No active elevation. No resisted work. If subscapularis repaired: no active IR and no passive ER beyond the specified limit (often 0–30°)
Wean the sling; active-assisted progressing to active range; full passive range; gentle submaximal isometrics toward the end
No heavy lifting; no resisted strengthening until phase III
Progressive resistance: ER, IR, scaption, rows, serratus and lower trapezius; progress load gradually
Avoid rapid, high-load or end-range provocative work
Overhead loading, energy-storage work, graded sport or work exposure

content.label: Evidence note
content.text:
Early versus delayed motion after repair has been studied extensively. Meta-analyses generally find that early passive motion produces better range in the first few months with no meaningful long-term difference, and may increase re-tear rates in large and massive tears.
Delayed protocols do not appear to cause lasting stiffness in most patients.
The practical synthesis: stratify by tear size and tissue quality. Small repairs in good tissue tolerate earlier motion; large, retracted or poor-quality repairs justify protection.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
The two commonest post-operative rehabilitation errors are opposite, and both are avoidable.
Progressing active loading too early risks the repair in its weakest window. Excessive immobilisation beyond protocol produces a stiff shoulder that then takes months to treat.
Ask the surgeon two questions for every post-operative patient: what exactly was repaired, and what are the range limits and the timeline? Write the answers in the notes. A protocol followed without knowing the tear size and the tissue quality is a guess with a schedule attached.
13.5 Massive irreparable tears — the conservative programme that works

content.body:
Patients with massive irreparable tears are often told nothing can be done short of reverse arthroplasty. That is wrong for a substantial proportion of them.

The principle: if the cuff cannot restore the fulcrum, train the anterior deltoid to elevate the arm in a position where it can. The deltoid's line of pull becomes more effective as the arm moves away from the vertical, so the programme begins supine, where gravity does not demand a fulcrum, and progresses through inclined positions toward upright.

rows: Begin without load; add small weights (0.5–1 kg) as control improves
Advance the incline only when the current angle is controlled
Gradually add load; expect months, not weeks
Scapular control, posterior cuff where present, thoracic mobility, pain management

content.body:
Realistic expectations: many patients regain functional elevation and meaningful reduction in disability. Those with true pseudoparalysis, fixed superior migration and established cuff tear arthropathy are more likely to need reverse total shoulder arthroplasty, which reconstructs the fulcrum by moving the centre of rotation and letting deltoid do the work.

Other surgical options for the massive irreparable tear include debridement, partial repair, superior capsular reconstruction and tendon transfer; indications remain debated and outcomes are variable.

content.text: 14. Outcome measures and benchmarks

content.body: Measure something. "Better" is not an outcome, and it will not survive a clinic letter, a return-to-work discussion or an insurance query.

content.text: 14.1 Patient-reported measures

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: The 2025 guideline grades this A: use valid, reliable and responsive patient-reported questionnaires to assess pain and disability — naming SPADI, DASH/QuickDASH and ASES among suitable options.

content.body: Choose one and use it consistently. MCID values vary between studies and populations — treat them as approximate thresholds for "the patient would notice this", not as precise cut-offs.

content.text: 14.2 Physical benchmarks

rows: Inclinometer or app, not visual estimate
LSI >90% for return to heavy or overhead demand
Sustained or repeated task at height, counted
The actual provocative task, graded by volume

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Measure at baseline, 6 weeks and 12 weeks, the same way each time.
Three data points are enough to answer the only question that matters at review: is capacity rising? If pain has not changed but ER strength has risen 30%, the programme is working and needs time. If neither has changed in eight weeks, go to the troubleshooting sequence in 11.12 — do not simply extend the same programme for another eight weeks.
15. Prognosis and communication
15.1 What to expect

content.body:
• Most patients improve with conservative management, but recovery is measured in months, and a substantial minority have persistent symptoms at one year.
  • Degenerative tears may enlarge over time, particularly full-thickness tears, though not all do and enlargement does not always mean symptoms.
  • Recurrence is common if load rises again without capacity being maintained — which is the argument for a maintenance dose rather than discharge to nothing.

Poor prognostic factors: longer symptom duration, higher baseline pain and disability, diabetes, smoking, psychosocial factors (low expectation of recovery, fear-avoidance, workers' compensation context), high work demands, and larger tears with fatty infiltration.

content.text: 15.2 The consultation as an intervention

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text:
Expectation of recovery is among the stronger predictors of outcome — which means the way you explain this condition is part of the treatment, not the preamble to it.
Say: "This is a tendon that has been asked to do more than it can currently manage. We build its capacity back up — it takes a few months, and it works."
Avoid: "Your tendon is torn and worn out, and it's being pinched by the bone." That sentence is mechanistically outdated, and it predicts a worse outcome.
15.3 Answering the three questions patients actually ask

rows: "We can, and sometimes we should. But at your age the scan will almost certainly show some wear, which is also true of people with no pain at all. It would change what you believe more than what we do. If you're not improving in about twelve weeks, that's the point at which the scan starts to earn its place."

"Most people with this don't. The operation that used to be done for it turned out to perform no better than a placebo operation. Repairing an actual tear is a different question, and if you don't improve with proper loading we'll reconsider — choosing to rehabilitate first doesn't close that door."

"An injection will probably take the pain down for six to eight weeks. It doesn't change the tendon. So it's useful if we use that window to do the strengthening — but on its own, the pain usually comes back, because nothing has changed about what the tendon can handle."

content.text: 16. Worked cases

content.body: Four cases, chosen because each turns on a different reasoning step. Cover the right-hand column and work them through.

content.text: 16.1 The painter

content.body: A 54-year-old decorator presents with four weeks of right lateral shoulder pain. It began the week after he finished a large ceiling job. Pain is 7/10 overhead, wakes him most nights, settles over an hour or two after activity. Active elevation is limited by pain at 110°; passive elevation is full. Painful arc present. No lag signs. ER strength is reduced but painful. Cervical screen is normal.

rows: Yes — lateral pain, painful arc, full passive range, normal cervical screen
No lag signs; weakness is painful rather than absent. No early imaging needed
High — night pain most nights, provoked easily, settles over hours
Reactive-on-degenerative — a clear overload event on a 54-year-old tendon
Full overhead occupational work, sustained, for hours

Stage 1 for 2 weeks (isometrics, sleep positioning, modified work at bench height). Then staged loading. Occupational health involvement for a graded return. Full programme to 12 weeks minimum, with the final stage building overhead endurance, not just strength

content.body: Teaching point: the temptation is to image and inject. The history already gives the diagnosis, and the correct first move is unloading plus an achievable starting dose — with the work situation addressed in parallel, because the job is the load.

content.text: 16.2 The fall

content.body: A 46-year-old cyclist fell onto the shoulder nine days ago. Immediate pain, and since then she cannot lift the arm. Passive elevation is full and comfortable; active elevation is 60°. External rotation lag sign is positive. No neck pain, normal cervical screen, no sensory change.

rows: Yes — positive lag sign, trauma, immediate loss of active function with full passive range. This is the finding that changes the pathway
Urgent imaging and early surgical referral. Delay allows retraction and fatty infiltration, which are not reversed by later repair
Neurological — axillary or suprascapular nerve injury, neuralgic amyotrophy. Check deltoid and the sensory patch; if weakness is disproportionate or non-cuff in pattern, consider EMG
Maintain passive range; analgesia; do not enrol in a 12-week loading programme and review in three months

content.body: Teaching point: traumatic, young-ish, immediate weakness, positive lag sign — this is one of the few presentations where delay actually costs outcome.

content.text: 16.3 The incidental tear

content.body: A 71-year-old retired teacher had an MRI arranged by her GP for six months of aching shoulder pain. It reports a 2 cm full-thickness supraspinatus tear with Goutallier grade 2 change. She is distressed by the report and has stopped using the arm. Active elevation is 150° with a painful arc; passive is full. No lag sign. She wants to know when she can have it repaired.

rows: Not necessarily — full-thickness tears are common and frequently asymptomatic at this age, and she retains near-full active elevation with no lag sign
No. Degenerative, no acute trauma, preserved function
Arguably the report and the resulting avoidance, as much as the tendon

Reframe the imaging explicitly (8.4). Begin loading at a genuine dose — low irritability means underdosing is the main risk. Outcome measure at baseline and 12 weeks. Revisit surgery only if function fails to improve with real loading

content.body: Teaching point: this case is won or lost in the explanation. If she leaves believing her shoulder is broken and waiting for a repair, no programme will be done properly.

content.text: 16.4 The thrower

content.body: A 22-year-old javelin thrower has six months of posterior shoulder pain in late cocking. Full range except internal rotation at 90° reduced by 25° compared with the other side. Scapular dyskinesis on lowering, and the scapular assistance test reduces his pain. Strong but painful ER. No lag signs. He has had two steroid injections elsewhere, each helping for a month.

rows: Rotator cuff related, but consider internal impingement and posterior labral pathology given position-specific pain in late cocking
Low to moderate — pain is provoked by a specific high-demand position
A measured IR deficit, a positive symptom modification test, and a sport whose demand is speed, not just load
They treated the symptom, not the capacity, and the throwing volume never changed

Posterior mobility work (because it was measured and modifiable), scapular control (because the assistance test was positive), heavy slow loading of the posterior cuff — and then stage 4 is compulsory: energy storage, deceleration control, kinetic chain, and a counted throwing progression

content.body: Teaching point: this is the patient most likely to be under-rehabilitated, because he will feel fine at the end of stage 3 and go back to full throwing. The relapse happens in week two of the season.

content.text: 17.2 Fifteen pearls

content.body:
1. "Impingement" is an outdated causal model. Think capacity versus load.
  2. Ask what changed in the month before onset, not what happened on the day.
  3. Irritability sets the dose; diagnosis sets the direction.
  4. The cuff is a compressor first — dysfunction is loss of a fulcrum, not loss of one movement.
  5. Supraspinatus does not "initiate the first 15°." Stop teaching it.
  6. Lag signs beat pain tests — they indicate structural failure rather than sensitisation.
  7. Passive range is the discriminator from adhesive capsulitis.
  8. Screen the cervical spine every time. C5 radiculopathy often has no neck pain.
  9. Imaging findings are age-related and common. A tear on a scan is not a diagnosis, and the report changes beliefs more than management.
  10. Use a dynamometer, not manual muscle testing, and record the numbers.
  11. Tendon adapts on a 12-week timeline; patients feel better at six. Say so in advance — that gap is where relapse happens.
  12. The commonest cause of a failed programme is a dose that never progressed.
  13. A flare means a smaller dose, not no dose.
  14. Subacromial decompression did not beat placebo surgery. Repair for the right tear still has a role, and a traumatic tear in a younger patient should be referred early.
  15. Massive irreparable tear is not the end of rehabilitation — the anterior deltoid programme restores useful function in many patients.

content.text: 17.3 Red flags

content.body:
• Acute traumatic tear with marked weakness or a positive lag sign in a younger patient → early surgical referral
  • Weakness without pain → neurological: suprascapular neuropathy, C5 radiculopathy, neuralgic amyotrophy, motor neuron disease
  • Severe pain preceding patchy weakness → neuralgic amyotrophy
  • Pain completely unaffected by active and passive movement → referred: cervical, cardiac, diaphragmatic, apical lung (Pancoast)
  • Constitutional symptoms, night pain with a cancer history, a mass → image for malignancy
  • Hot, swollen, systemically unwell → septic arthritis; aspirate before any steroid
  • Progressive atrophy without trauma → entrapment, mass lesion, or motor neuron disease

content.text: 17.4 The chapter on one page

content.body:
1. Is it the cuff? → history pattern, passive range, cervical screen
  2. Structural failure? → lag signs, trauma, weakness without pain
  3. How irritable? → sets the starting dose
  4. What is the target? → sets the endpoint
Then: EXPLAIN → UNLOAD → RELOAD → FIX THE BACKGROUND
Not working at 6–8 weeks? Diagnosis · dose · adherence · outside load · reactivity → background health · sensitisation · then image.
